"Angle of attack" is the angle the wing is traveling through the air. If it was purely knifing through the air, leading edge same height as trailing edge, lift would be considerably less than when there is some angle, the leading edge is higher than the trailing edge.

However at some point when the angle of attack is too great, flow becomes turbulent, and lift decreases drastically. (Stall.)

The pilot controls angle of attack with the stick, which changes the amount of lift (actually usually downforce) from the tail, thus angling the entire aircraft as the means of angling the wing. The pilot should be able to avoid excessive AOA simply by flying correctly, but pilots err and for this reason aircraft have been equipped with stick pushers to automatically "push the nose down" when AOA becomes excessive.

The 737 Max used only one of its AOA sensors to control its system, even though they have two sensors (Boeing made it an extra cost option for the system to alert when the two sensors disagreed, and Lion Air chose not to buy that option, which obviously should have been standard not extra cost.)
